3.x: Jesus opens up with the Beatitudes (Beatitude comes from the Latin word “beantitudo”, which means “blessedness” or “happiness”). “Blessed (“beati” in the Latin Vulgate)”: comes from the Greek word “makarios”, and it can also mean fortunate or happy. However, in this context, the word means more than “happy”, since happiness is an emotion often dependent on outward circumstances. “Poor in spirit”: in contrast with the proud and self-sufficient. This speaks of the deep humility of recognizing one’s utter spiritual bankruptcy apart from God. It describes those who are acutely conscious of their own lostness and hopelessness apart from divine grace. Jesus was teaching that the kingdom is a gracious gift to those who sense their own poverty of spirit. This verse is the direct opposite of the Pharisee’s mindset: “Blessed am I, for I have kept the law, I fast twice a week, and I am spiritually wealthy.” Yet, the poor is Spirit: “Lord, I have nothing to offer. If you don’t provide life, I will wither away.”

4.x: “they that mourn (KJV)”: the Greek word for “mourn” is “pentheo”, which is the strongest word for grief that goes beyond sadness - to lament. When the world tells you to avoid pain and seek constant entertainment, Jesus tells you to lean into the grief, for there is where God will meet you. When the world tells you that mourning is a sign of weakness, Jesus tells you that it is a sign of a heart that is alive.

5.x: The Greek word for “meek” is “prays”. And it means the gentle, meek, humble, or lowly. It is not weakness, but supreme self-control empowered by the Spirit. “Inherit the earth”: the Greek word for “earth” is “ge”, and it could also mean “land”, depending on context. Preterists (those who interpret Revelation as events that have already occurred during the destruction of the Temple in 70AC as opposed to future eschatological events) prefer the rendering of land (referring to Israel) instead of earth (referring to the world).

6.x: Jesus moves from the “internal” feelings of poverty and mourning to a powerful, active drive for righteousness. “Those who hunger & thirst for righteousness”: people that are starving for the entirety of God’s will to be done on earth and in their own hearts. They are not imposing their own righteousness, but looking(starving) for God’s righteousness.

7.x: Mercy is higher than Justice (Jms 2:13). If we received Justice, no one would be saved. We are dependent on mercy. If we want to receive mercy and be forgiven by our Father, we MUST forgive those who have sinned against us. Forgiveness is a salvation matter (Mt 6:14-15). Give mercy and you will receive mercy.

8.x: The Greek word for “pure” is “katharon”, which means “unmixed”, “pure”, “clean”. Like 100% pure gold or wine that has no sediment. A pure heart isn’t a “perfect” heart; it is a heart with a SINGLE motive. It isn’t trying to serve “two masters” (Mt 6:24).

9.x: “the peacemakers (KJV)”: not just the peace-keepers, but the MAKERS of peace. Jesus is the ultimate peacemaker who reconciled us to the Father.

10.x: “persecuted for righteousness (KJV)”: you would think that a “pure-hearted peacemaker” would be loved by everyone. But Jesus warns that the world often hates the “Light” (Jn 3:19). This blessing isn’t for those who are “persecuted” for being rude or difficult. It is for those who are treated poorly specifically because they are abiding in the character of Jesus.

13.x: To be “salt”, a follower of Jesus has to perform three specific jobs in the word: (1) Preservation (stopping the rot) - while we are on this Earth, we help “preserve” the Earth from falling into pure corruption. (2) Flavor - a Christian who is “abiding” should make life more “savory” and joyful for those around them. (3) Thirst (Creating desire) - salt makes you thirsty. The life of a “pure-hearted” (v 8) believer should make others “hunger and thirst” (v 6) for righteousness as well. This connects directly to the Beatitudes. When you are “Merciful” (v 7), you “preserve” relationships through forgiveness. When you are a “Peacemaker” (v 9), you bring flavor to a bitter, divided community. When you are “Persecuted” (v 11), you stay “salty” even when the world tries to wash you away. “If the salt loses its flavor”: scientifically, pure Sodium Chloride (salt) cannot lose its saltiness. However, the salt in Galilee was often gathered from the Dead Sea and was mixed with white dust and minerals. If the salt got wet (diluted), the actual sodium chloride would leach out, leaving behind a white powder that looked like salt but had no flavor or preservative power. This is the same thing as the “Lord, Lord” warning of Mt 7:21-23. If a Christian tries to mix the “sap” of the Vine with the “Iniquity” of the world, they become “diluted.” They have the appearance of salt, but they have lost their saltiness and will ultimately be thrown out and trampled.

17.x: “the law, or the prophets”: the Law refers to the first five books (the Torah), and the prophets include the rest of the OT, all of which was held to have been written by prophets. “not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets”: Jesus did not come to abolish or cancel the Law or the Prophets. He is not against what came before. He came to fulfill, which means to complete, to bring to its intended goal, to perfect and fully reveal its meaning: (1) He fulfills its prophecies. Christ is the reality that the promises, shadows and types anticipated; (2) He fulfills its true meaning. In the verses that follow (Mt 5:21-48), he shows that the Law is deeper than outward actions, it reaches the heart. For example, it’s not just “don’t murder”, but “don’t hate”. It’s not just “don’t commit adultery”, but “don’t lust.” (3) He fulfills it through perfect obedience. He alone kept the Law perfectly & without sin (1 Peter 2:22; 1 Jn 3:5; Heb 4:15; 2 Cor 5:21). Only he was worthy to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessings as the only sinless man (Rev 5:12; Phil 2:5-8). This means that Mary is not the sinless person that Catholics claim. The Bible is very clear that “ALL HAVE SINNED, and come short of the glory of God” (Rom 3:23). Mary even performs a “sin offering” (Lk 2:24; Lev 12:8). See notes on Luke 1:28 for more on Mary’s supposed sinlessness. (4) He fulfills its sacrificial system. The Law required sacrifices and offerings, and Christ became the final sacrifice as the Lamb of God: “one sacrifice for sins for ever” (Heb 10:12 KJV). Now “there is no more offering for sin” (Heb 10:18 KJV). This means that the propitiatory(for sins) sacrificial view of the Eucharist in Catholic Churches is a lie and gives people a false sense of forgiveness of sins. They turned salvation into a time-based achievement, being saved at noon after Mass, & being condemned for Purgatory (potentially even hell) at 11am before Mass. The Catholic Church goes even further and added to its Canon Law (Canon 1247) that “on Sundays and other holy days of obligation, the faithful are obliged to participate in the Mass.” Code of Canon Law, Canon 920 S1 says: “each of the faithful is obliged to receive holy communion AT LEAST ONCE A YEAR.” Also similarly stated in their Catechism paragraph 2024 - “but in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mt 15:9 KJV). Salvation is not works-based (Eph 2:8-9; Rom 3:28; 4:5; 5:1; Gal 2:16;), so anyone who teaches otherwise is not of God, and leads people into perdition: “Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law; YE ARE FALLEN FROM GRACE” (Gal 5:4 KJV). We are ALL royal priesthood for “SPIRITUAL SACRIFICES” (1 Peter 2:5 KJV). The bloody sacrifices (Heb 9:22) of the OT are fulfilled in Jesus, and since there are no more sacrifices left to make, the job of an actual priest is irrelevant now. After Jesus’ death, the veil that separated people from the Holy of Holies got torn in two (Mk 15:37-38). We can now all approach God to offer spiritual sacrifices as His royal priesthood. These include: (1) a living sacrifice of our bodies/lives (Rom 12:1); (2) the sacrifice of praise with the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name (Heb 13:15); (3) doing good and sharing (Heb 13:16); (4) prayer (Ps 141:2), etc etc. The Eucharist cannot be a sacrifice because sacrifices are no longer needed, if anything, it’d be a “Spiritual” sacrifice that we do towards God for love, not necessity (and it wouldn’t even work as a sacrifice since for a sacrifice to remit sin, there must be shedding of blood [Heb 9:22]). The Eucharist is a “memorial” - that is, something we are to do “in remembrance” (or “in memory”) of Jesus and His sacrifice (Lk 22:19; 1 Cor 11:24-25). You cannot have a “memorial” if the person you are “remembering” or "memorializing" is right there with you. Also, drinking blood is prohibited in the Bible before the Law (Gen 9:4), during the Law (Lev 17:10-12), and after the Law (Acts 15:20). It would be unthinkable for the apostles to treat the Last Supper as Jesus’ actual blood. Jesus almost always spoke in parables & metaphors. In fact, that was his norm, so much that when he did not speak in parables, his apostles were impressed: “now speakest thou plainly, and speakest no proverb” (Jn 16:29 KJV). In the book of John, Jesus states his seven “I AM”: (1) I am the Bread of Life (Jn 6:35); (2) I am the Light of the World (Jn 8:12); (3) I am the Door (Jn 10:9); (4) I am the Good Shepherd (Jn 10:11); (5) I am the Resurrection and the Life (Jn 11:25); (6) I am the Way, the Truth, and the Life (Jn 14:6); (7) I am the True Vine (Jn 15:1). It would be foolish, and violence to Scripture to treat them all as symbolic, except when he says “I am the bread of life” (Jn 6:35).

18.x: “one jot or one tittle”: a jot (iota in Greek, or yod in Hebrew) refers to the smallest letter in the alphabet, and a tittle refers to a tiny stroke - meaning that not even the smallest detail of the Law will fail to come about. Christ was affirming the utter inerrancy and absolute authority of the OT as the Word of God- down to the smallest stroke or letter. This suggests that the NT should not be seen as supplanting or repealing the OT, but as fulfilling and explicating it. For example, all the ceremonial requirements of the Mosaic Law were fulfilled in Christ and are no longer to be observed by Christians (Col 2:16-17). Everything written in the Law (commands, promises, types and shadows) must reach its full completion. Christ is the one who brings that fulfillment, bringing the Law to completion and giving it the correct understanding.

19.x: “break one of these least commandments”: (1) “least”: even commandments that seem small or minor; (2) “break”: to loosen, disregard, or set aside. Hence, no command of God is to be treated as insignificant. “And shall teach men so”: it’s not only about personal disobedience, but also influencing others to do the same. Teaching error increases accountability. “Shall be called least in the kingdom”: we are not saved by works, so breaking God’s law does not necessarily mean losing your salvation. If that was the case, absolutely no one would be saved. Rather, we will be rewarded according to our works, and if your works are not good (“wood, hay, stubble” instead of “gold, silver, precious stones”), you will be given the position of least honor in the Kingdom of God (1 Cor 3:12-15). However, “shall we sin, because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid!” (Rom 6:14-16 KJV). “Whosoever shall do and teach them”: we cannot judge others nor teach others unless we obey ourselves (Mt 7:5). God does not want us to keep our faith to ourselves, but to share it to all the nations, beginning in your own home: “thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up” (Deut 6:6-7 KJV), “we will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and His strength, and His wonderful works that He hath done” (Ps 78:4 KJV), “preach the Word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2 Tim 4:2 KJV), “daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ” (Acts 5:42 KJV), “woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!” (1 Cor 9:16 KJV), “preach the gospel to every creature” (Mk 16:15 KJV), etc.

20.x: These are weighty words from Jesus, and they would have shocked His hearers. The Scribes and Pharisees were seen as the most righteous people in society: they were experts in the Law, strict observers of religious rules, and highly respected for outward holiness. To the people, they were the standard of righteousness. “Except your righteousness shall exceed…”: Jesus is saying: “Unless your righteousness goes beyond theirs, you will not enter the kingdom.” This is not a small improvement, it is a completely higher kind of righteousness. God demands perfection (Mt 5:48). Without perfection no one will enter the Kingdom of God. Since perfection is impossible for men (Rom 3:23), this means that righteousness is produced by God and given to men. “With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible” (Mt 19:26 KJV). Human effort alone cannot reach that perfection, so God makes possible what man cannot achieve through Jesus Christ. When we get baptized in Jesus’ name (Acts 2:38), we “put on Christ” (Gal 3:27 KJV). God does not judge us by our works anymore, but by Jesus’ perfection. When we accept BY FAITH Jesus as our savor and obey His Word by baptizing, “we are buried with him” (Rom 6:4 KJV), and are reborn to walk in “newness of life” (Rom 6:4 KJV). This is equivalent to the Israelites placing the lamb’s blood on their doorposts (Ex 12:13). The angel of death did not go into the house to see what they were doing, he simply looked at the lamb’s blood outside and the people inside were justified. Likewise, we are not judged by our works, but are justified before the Father by “putting on” Jesus in baptism. The plan of salvation is not perfection, it is Acts 2:28 KJV: “Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ FOR THE REMISSION(forgiveness) OF SINS.” Repentance & baptism are salvation issues (Mk 16:16; Lk 13:3; 1 Peter 3:21). This is why the yoke of Jesus is easy (Mt 11:28-30), because it is no longer our righteousness, but His righteousness that saves us. Jeremiah prophesied about this: “and this is His name whereby He shall be called, The LORD(YHWH) Our Righteousness (remember Jesus means YHWH-saves)” (Jer 23:6 KJV). This is also why the least in the kingdom of God is greater than John the Baptist (the greatest man to be born of a woman [Mt 11:11]), because we possess the blessing of experiencing the new birth, union with Christ, the indwelling Spirit, and the imputed righteousness of God. The new birth makes kingdom citizens spiritually greater. Jesus told Nicodemus: “Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” (Jn 3:3 KJV). And: “That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.” (Jn 3:6 KJV). Under the New Covenant, believers are regenerated by the Spirit and become new creations (2 Cor 5:17). Believers receive God’s own righteousness. The Pharisees had external righteousness, but Christ gives a righteousness from God (Jer 23:6). Paul explains this righteousness is given through faith: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” (2 Cor 5:21 KJV). And: “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ” (Phil 3:9 KJV). So the “least” believer in Christ possesses something greater than even the greatest prophet under the law. The indwelling Holy Spirit (God, YHWH, the Father, the divine Spirit of Jesus) is a greater covenant privilege: “for the Holy Ghost was not yet given; because that Jesus was not yet glorified” (Jn 7:39 KJV). After Christ’s glorification in his resurrection, believers receive the Spirit internally: “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Col 1:27 KJV). And “your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost” (1 Cor 6:19 KJV). This truth is a salvation issue. If anyone thinks that his actions will earn him heaven, he will not receive the righteousness from Christ: “Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law; ye are fallen from grace.” (Gal 5:4 KJV). Our “good works” are merely “filthy rags” before the perfect God (Isa 64:6).

40.x: “If any man will sue thee.. And take away thy coat..”: this refers to a legal dispute. The “coat” (tunic) was an inner garment. The “cloak” was an outer garment, more valuable, and even protected under the Law (Ex 22:26-27). “Let him have thy cloak also”: Jesus is not promoting injustice, but teaching to not cling to your things with a contentious spirit. Instead, be willing to yield more than required. Value peace and righteousness above possessions. When the world says: “fight for every right”, Jesus says: “be willing to surrender for the sake of peace.” This is about letting go of greed, pride, and vindictiveness & about not escalating conflict over material things.

41.x: “Whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile…”: this refers to a Roman practice where soldiers could force a civilian to carry gear for one mile. It was resented and seen as oppression by many Jews. Jesus teaches that instead of resentment & bare-minimum compliance, you should be willing and even generous in cooperation. The principle is to do more than what is forced upon you, and to turn compulsion into voluntary kindness. This will break the cycle of bitterness & give evidence of a transformed heart. Do not respond to wrong with resistance rooted in pride or revenge. Instead, yield where possible, give more than required, and act from love, not resentment.

42.x: Christians should help those who are truly needy (and therefore forced to beg), but they are not required to give foolishly (Mt 7:6), or to a lazy person who is not in need (2 Thess 3:10), or where giving would harm rather than benefit. It DOES NOT mean to give to absolutely anyone who asks. But, as with prior verses, he is addressing the heart posture, not laying down a law without wisdom. Believers are called to be wise stewards (Lk 16:10) & to care for their own households (1 Tim 5:8). However, we must never ignore the needy, avoid responsibility, nor harden oneself emotionally. Rather, imitate God, who gives freely (Mt 7:11) and who is merciful to the undeserving.

48.x: This verse is the conclusion of turning the other cheek, loving enemies, and giving freely. The word “perfect” (Greek: teleios) can mean: complete, mature, fully developed. The kingdom of God demands perfection. Remember that Jesus said that our righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, whom the people regarded as the most righteous people of society (v 20). Christ is setting an unattainable standard. This sums up what the law itself demanded: perfection. “For whoever keeps the whole law and yet stumbles in ONE POINT, he has become guilty of all” (Jms 2:10 KJV). Even the apostles were “exceedingly amazed” at his incredibly high standards: “Who then can be saved?" (Mt 19:25 KJV). Though this standard is impossible to meet, God could not lower it without compromising his own perfection. He who is perfect could not set an imperfect standard of righteousness. The marvelous truth of the gospel is that Christ has met this standard on our behalf: “For He hath made Him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor 5:21 KJV). This is why no one is saved by works (Eph 2:8-9), because no one would be saved if that was the case, as “ALL have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Rom 3:23). THIS IS CRUCIAL, this is a salvation issue. We must acknowledge our sinful nature and inability to earn salvation by our own efforts and be like babes dependent 100% on our Father for salvation: “Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Mt 18:3 KVJ). We have to be like the publican (tax collector), who “would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner.” (Lk 18:13-14 KJV). Like that man, if we acknowledge our depravity before God, He promises to be merciful & oversee our sin through the work of Jesus. Jesus is the true vine, and we are the branches, all we have to do is “abide” in His teachings (Jn 15:1,5), and he’ll take care of providing the fruits. Whoever thinks he deserves salvation for his own “good works”, he has “fallen from grace” (Gal 5:4), meaning he has lost his salvation, since “all our righteousness are as filthy rags” before the perfect God (Isa 64:6 KJV).

1-2.x: Jesus begins his famous Sermon on the Mount. The primary audience are the disciples. Matthew is very specific: Jesus sat down, and HIS DISCIPLES CAME TO HIM. In the ancient world, when a Rabbi sat down, it was a signal that a formal, deep teaching was beginning. However, while he is speaking mainly to the disciples, the “large crowds” from Galilee, Decapolis, Jerusalem, and Syria are still there, listening in from the perimeter. By the end of the sermon (Mt 7:28), the text says: “the people were astonished at his doctrine (KJV).”

11-12.x: Jesus moves from “blessed are those” to “blessed are YOU.” He moves from a high-level philosophy of the heart, to the immediate reality His disciples would face. “For my sake”: this is the qualifier, if people dislike you because you are rude or arrogant, there is no “Beatitude” in that. The blessing only applies when the world reacts negatively to you abiding in Jesus. “Rejoice and be exceedingly glad”: Jesus doesn’t say “endure it” or “grind your teeth through it.” He says to be exceedingly glad (agallio in Greek, meaning to jump for joy). Why? Because persecution is the membership card to an elite group. Jesus reminds his disciples that they are now in the same “vineyard” as Elijah, Jeremiah, and Isaiah. The “Great Light” has always been resisted by the darkness. If the world is attacking your faith, it is proof that you are abiding correctly. Every insult, every injustice done to you for the sake of Jesus is a deposit in your heavenly bank. Those who seek reward on Earth (like the Pharisees who wanted the best seats in the synagogues) have already received their payment in full. Those who wait for the Father’s reward are the ones who truly trust the Vine.

Ironically, each beatitude characterizes an exceedingly undesirable position in this world and calls it “blessed.” For example, those who mourn (v 4) are those who have suffered grief; those who are merciful (v 7) are those who have been wronged and offended; those who are peacemakers (v 9) are those who have had to enter into the fray and diffuse a dangerous situation. The world commonly deems the people who are troubled on every side as unfortunate or unlucky - having incurred, for some known or unknown reason, the wrath of God, the gods, or fate. Jesus, however, reversed these stigmas: those who have fallen out of favor with the predominant culture for the sake of following Christ are in reality the most fortunate members of society.

14-16.x: Jesus tells his disciples what they ought to be: the light of the world. Since Christ himself said he is the “light of the world” (Jn 8:12), as believers, we must be reflecting truth, exposing darkness (sin, error), & guiding others toward God as bearers of His light. “A city that is set on an hill (KJV)” is visible from afar & impossible to conceal. Our life as followers of Jesus must be one of PUBLIC testimony. “Let your light so shine before men (KJV)”: live in such a way that your actions reflect righteousness & visibly differentiated from darkness. But notice that the goal IS NOT attention, praise, self-exaltation, or salvation (since we’re not saved by works [Eph 2:8-9]). The goal is “that they may see your good works, and GLORIFY YOUR FATHER.”

Throughout church history, Catholicism has taught that Jesus’ words: “you are the salt of the world” and “you are the light of the world” was only meant to the disciples and Roman clergy. For example, in his Catena Aurea on Gospel of Matthew 5:13–16, Aquinas compiles patristic comments where “salt” is often tied to teachers who season others with doctrine and preserve from corruption: especially bishops and preachers. John Chrysostom says Christ is speaking especially to those entrusted with teaching the world. Since the apostles are being commissioned, “salt” and “light” are often applied to their public ministry. Jerome also often reads “salt” as doctrine and wisdom communicated by those who teach. So in Catholic commentary, these verses were frequently applied in a special sense to apostles, bishops, priests, and teachers. HOWEVER, Jesus is speaking to the disciples generally, not a clerical class. Matthew opens the sermon with: “And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain… and his disciples came unto him: And he opened his mouth, and taught them…” (Mt 5:1–2 KJV). Then: “Ye are the salt of the earth…” (v.13) & “Ye are the light of the world…” (v.14). At this point there is no ordained Christian clergy yet. No priests, bishops, or presbyters in the later ecclesial sense. He is addressing disciples, all of us. The “ye” of salt/light is the same audience as: “Blessed are the poor in spirit…”; “Blessed are the meek…”; “Blessed are the merciful…”; “Blessed are the peacemakers…” (v. 3-11). NO ONE ARGUES THOSE APPLY ONLY TO CLERGY. Then Jesus continues seamlessly: “ye are the salt… ye are the light” (v.13-14). The purpose clause includes ordinary visible works, not only preaching. Jesus explains: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (v. 16). Not merely sermons. Not only sacramental ministry. But good works visible in ordinary life (things that every believer does). The NT repeats this language for all believers: “That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God… among whom ye shine as lights in the world” (Phil 2:15 KJV) - Paul says this to the WHOLE church at Philippi, not clergy only. “Ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood… that ye should shew forth the praises of him…” (1 Peter 2:9 KJV) - Peter too, addresses all believers, not just clergy. “Now are ye light in the Lord: walk as children of light” (Eph 5:8 KJV) - Paul explicitly tells ALL BELIEVERS that they are the light, not clergy only. So as “the light”, Jesus says that we cannot be hidden: “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel…” (Mt 5:15 KJV). This applies to EVERY Christian life. Every disciple has a public witness - at home, at the marketplace, in our families, and in our communities.

21-22.x: Jesus is not changing the Law, he is revealing its true meaning. He contrasts “Ye have heard…” (common teaching) with “But I say unto you…” (true meaning). “Thou shalt not kill” comes from Ex 20:13, and the common understanding was that as long as you don’t commit murder, you’re righteous. However, Jesus goes deeper than than, into the heart. “Whosoever is angry…”: Jesus teaches that sin begins inside, not just in outward actions. Unjust anger is the root of murder, the same spirit, though not the same act. “Raca” is an Arameic term that means “empty-headed” or “worthless”, it shows contempt toward another person. “Thou fool”: is a stronger insult, it attacks a person’s character or worth. This reveals a hardened, hateful heart. Jesus shows a progression: Anger → Raca → Fool = judgement → council → hell fire. Not just actions, but words and attitudes matter. Jesus is saying that the Law is not only about outward behavior, but also inward thoughts, attitudes, speech. Murder begins in the heart.

Matthew 5:21 reads: “Thou shalt not kill (phoneuō).. (KJV)” or “do not murder(phoneuō)... (BSB).” phoneuō means “to murder”, “to commit UNLAWFUL killing”. It is used for intentional, unjust taking of life, not the general word for all killing. For example, the same word is also used in Mt 23:31 BSB: “So you testify against yourselves that you are the sons of those who MURDERED(phoneuō) the prophets.” The other Greek word for killing is apokteinō, which means “to kill” in general terms. It can include killing in war, execution, self-defense, etc. For example, this word is used in Mt 10:28 BSB: “Do not be afraid of those who KILL(apokteinō) the body but cannot KILL(apokteinō) the soul…” So in Mt 5:21, Jesus is quoting the commandment using a word that specifically means “murder”, not all killing. Likewise in Hebrew. In Ex 20:13: “Thou shalt not KILL(ratsach)”. The word “ratsach” means “to murder” or “to slay unlawfully” more specifically. This refers to premeditated murder or intentional killing with malice. For example: “he is a MURDERER(ratsach): the MURDERER(ratsach) shall surely be put to death” (Num 35:18 KJV). Contrasted with other Hebrew words that are less specific: (1) “harag” = to kill in general terms. For example: “And Cain… SLEW(harag) him” (Gen 4:8 KJV) → here it is used as “murder”, however, it can also be treated as non-specific killing, such as “For wrath KILLETH(harag) the foolish man” (Job 5:2 KJV). (2) “muth”: to die/ cause to die. For example: “in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely DIE(muth)” (Gen 2:17 KJV) → not killing, but the state of death; (3) “nakah” = to strike, smite. For example: “and [Moses] SMOTE(nakah) the waters” (Ex 7:20 KJV) → no death, just striking. And “He that SMITETH(nakah) a man, so that he DIE(muth)..” (Ex 21:12 KJV) → strike can lead to death. The Bible very clearly prohibits intentional, unlawful killing (premeditated) (ratsach & phoneuō). However, the Bible allows (or regulates) lawful killing, such as divinely sanctioned Warfare (Israel conquering land in the book of Joshua, or the command against Amalek in 1 Sam 15:3). Killing in war is often described with “harah”, not “ratsach.” Capital Punishment is also Biblically lawful before the Law (Gen 9:6), during the Law (Ex 21:12), and after the Law (Rom 13:1-4; Acts 25:11). The Bible also allows for self-defense (Ex 22:2; Lk 11:21; 22:36; 1 Tim 5:8 ), and accidental killing (Num 35:11-12; Deut 19:5). What God despises is the shedding of INNOCENT BLOOD (Prov 6:16-17; Ps 94:21-23; Deut 19:10; Mt 23:35). God also despises manslayers going unpunished: “Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore, the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil” (Ecc 8:11 KJV). In the book of Numbers, God explains that the failure to execute a murderer “defiles” or “pollutes” the entire nation (Num 35:31,33). From a biblical perspective, a society that refuses to punish the shedding of blood becomes spiritually and morally “blood-guilty.” When the “judges” fail to act, the law becomes “slacked(ineffective)”: “Therefore the law is slacked(ineffective), and judgement doth never go forth: for the wicked doth compass about the righteous; therefore wrong judgement proceedeth” (Hab 1:4 KJV). Or “They that forsake the law praise the wicked: but such as keep the Law contend with them” (Prov 28:4 KJV). The Bible argues that the public execution of justice serves as a “warning” that keeps the rest of society from falling into the same corruption. Without the fear of consequences, the social fabric unravels: “...so shalt thou put the evil away from among you. And those which remain shall hear, and fear, and shall henceforth commit no more any such evil among you” (Deut 19:19-20 KVJ). In the NT, the focus shifts from a Theocracy (where the church and state are one) to a distinction between the Church and the Civil government. The NT DOES NOT abolish capital punishment, rather, it defines it as a function of the State to prevent the very societal corruption and “lawlessness” from spreading. “For rules are not a terror to good works, but to the evil…FOR HE BEARETH NOT THE SWORD IN VAIN: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to EXECUTE WRATH UPON HIM THAT DOETH EVIL” (Rom 13:3-4 KJV). If the “minister of God” (the government) refuses to use the sword and be a “terror to evil”, then evil men have no reason to fear, and the society inevitably becomes corrupted by those who no longer face consequence. The increase of lawlessness has its consequences: “Because of the multiplication of wickedness(lawlessness), the love of most will grow cold” (Mt 24:12 BSB). Mercy to the wicked is injustice to the righteous. When justice isn’t upheld, the “abundance of iniquity” causes a total breakdown of social love and trust. While the NT focuses heavily on grace for the individual, it maintains that for society to function, justice must be served to prevent the “leavening” (spreading) of sin: “Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners… for manslayers…and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine” (1 Tim 1:9-10 KJV). Paul argues that the law (and its penalties) is essential to restrain “manslayers.” If the law is not applied to them, the “sound doctrine” of a safe, godly society is compromised. Even at the Crucifixion, the NT records an admission that capital punishment is a “just” consequence for certain crimes to maintain the order of justice: “And we indeed justly; for we receive the DUE REWARD OF OUR DEEDS: but this man hath done nothing amiss” (Lk 23:41 KJV). The thief on the cross recognized that a society that does not give the “due reward” for crimes loses its sense of “justness.”

23-24.x: Jesus had just taught that anger and hatred is the root of murder, and therefore it is as unacceptable as the act of murder itself. He now goes further: even religious worship is unacceptable if relationships are broken. For Jesus, taking pains to see that one lives harmoniously with others is more sacred than many other forms of worship. “Rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee”: it doesn’t say “YOU have something against him”, but that HE has something against you. This implies that YOU have wronged HIM. Hence, the one who initiates the reconciliation here is the one who has wronged the other person. Before we approach God, we must first take care of our human responsibilities, such as being a peacemaker and taking care of our immediate family members. In Mark 7:9-13, the Pharisees would give money to God(Corban) and forsake their parents, and Jesus reprimanded them for twisting God’s Word. God’s command says: “honour thy father and mother” (Ex 20:12), and their tradition said: “you don’t have to help your parents if you declare it Corban(given to God)”. They used religion to avoid obedience. Jesus says they reject God’s commandment, replace it with human tradition, and make God’s Word void. It is nothing more than hypocrisy, hence: “if a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” (1 Jn 4:20 KJV).

25-26.x: In the immediate context, this continues the same theme from v 21-24: anger, conflict, and reconciliation. Jesus describes a legal scenario with: (1) Adversary: the one who has a case against you; (2) Judge: authority who decides; (3) Office: enforcer; (4) Prison: consequence of losing the case. The lesson is to “Agree.. Quickly,” to settle disputes early, don’t let conflict escalate. “While thou art in the way”: do it while there is a window of opportunity, for once judgement comes, it’s too late. “Cast into prison”: consequences become inescapable. “Till thou hast paid…”: full accountability, no escape without settling the debt. Jesus is teaching: MAKE THINGS RIGHT NOW. Reconcile quickly. Do not carry anger to judgement, because judgement will be strict, and delay leads to inescapable consequences. Reconciliation must not be postponed.

Since Catholics do not have Biblical support for Purgatory, they try to argue that this verse (Mt 5:25-26) is about purgatory, where the “prison” is the temporary place after death, and the “Till thou hast paid” refers to a finite punishment in Purgatory. Therefore, they believe Jesus is hinting at a place where souls are purified before entering heaven until all temporal punishment has been paid. However, this is neither apostolic teaching, nor Biblical, it was a clear human development hundreds of years after Jesus. For example, Augustine (430AC), son to a pagan father and a devout Christian mother, was one of the most influential Christian theologians and philosophers in Western history. Although he did not use the later medieval term of “purgatory”, he clearly SPECULATED about a potential post-death purification for certain saved souls. He wrote: “it is not impossible that something of the same kind may take place even after this life…whether some believers shall pass through a kind of purgatorial fire, and in proportion as they have loved with more or less devotion the goods that perish, be less or more quickly delivered from it.” (Enchiridion, Handbook on Faith, Hope, and Love, Ch 69). Augustine approached this with some caution- he presented post-death purification as plausible and worth inquiring into, not as an unquestioned dogma. However, Pope Gregory I (590-604AC), writing nearly 200 years later, removed the “maybe” and turned it into “certainty.” In his Dialogues, he stated flatly: “For certain light faults, we must believe that there is a purgatorial fire before the judgement.” Gregory didn’t just use logic, he used narrative. His Dialogues were some of the most widely read books in the Middle Ages(500-1500AC). They were filled with “first-hand” accounts of “visions” and “miracles”. For example, he wrote the story of Justus, whom Gregory describes as a monk who died with three gold coins (a sin against poverty). Gregory ordered 30 days of Mass for him, after which the monk’s soul appeared in a vision to say he was finally released from his torment. He also told the story of a deacon named Paschacius who was seen after his death serving at the baths as a form of penance. By using these relatable, often spooky stories, Gregory made the concept of a “middle state” terrifyingly real for the average person. Hence, Gregory was the first to strongly link the Mass to the release of souls from Purgatory. After Gregory, the idea emerged that a specific number of Masses (like the Gregorian Masses, a series of 30) could “buy” a soul’s way out of fire. This created a direct “transactional” relationship between the living and the dead that would dominate the Roman Church for the next millennium. Gregory was writing during the Dark Ages, a period full of plague, war, and the collapse of the Roman Empire. People were obsessed with death and the afterlife. Gregory’s concrete answers provided a sense of control over the “fate of the soul.” Gregory the Great is essentially the “Father of Purgatory.” This “theology of the afterlife” became the single most effective financial engine in the history of the Roman Catholic Church. While Rome had other sources of income (tithes, land ownership, and taxes from the Papal States), nothing compared to the “Economy of Grace” because it was universal and fueled by the most powerful human motivator: fear for one’s loved ones. After Gregory, wealthy nobles would leave massive endowments in their wills to build small chapels and pay a priest to do nothing but say “Private Masses” for their souls, every single day, forever. The “Gregorian Masses” became a standard package. If you wanted to ensure your father was out of Purgatory, you paid for a set of 30 consecutive Masses. The real “money-making machine” reached its peak with Indulgences. By the 1500s, the Roman Church was essentially selling “time off” from Purgatory to fund massive infrastructure projects. Johan Tetzel was the most famous “salesman” of this machine. His famous jingle was: “As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs.” The sheer volume of land and gold that flowed into Rome via testamentary bequests (wills) was staggering. By the late Middle Ages, the Roman Church owned nearly one-third of the land in Europe. Much of this land was given by people on their deathbeds in exchange for “perpetual Masses” to shorten their time in Purgatory. Of course, this financial system became so aggressive that it eventually triggered Martin Luther’s 95 Theses in 1517, unleashing the Protestant Reformation. While the Catholic Church reformed the sale of indulgences at the Council of Trent (1545AC), the theological link between the Mass and the relief of souls in Purgatory remains official Cahtolic doctrine today. Purgatory moved from “popular belief” to “official dogma” through three major councils: (1) Council of Lyon II (1274AC): the first official mention, affirming that souls are “purified by purgatorial pains and can be helped by the prayers of the living; (2) Council of Florence (1439AC): this was a major step, specifically addressing the “middle state” of souls who died in God’s grace but were still imperfect; (3) Council of Trent (1563AC): this was the definitive dogmatization. In response to the Protestant Reformation (which rejected Purgatory), the Church doubled down and issued the “Decree Concerning Purgatory”, which states: “There is a purgatory, and that the souls there detained are helped by the suffrages of the faithful, but principally by the acceptable sacrifice of the altar [the Mass].”

27-28.x: Jesus follows the same pattern, and gives true, deeper meaning to the misunderstood commandment of “thou shalt not commit adultery(Ex 20:14 KJV).” He moves from external (adultery), to the internal desire (lust). “Whosoever looketh… to lust after her…”: not every “looking” is sin, but the looking with intent to desire, a deliberate, cultivated lust. Lust is not mere attraction nor simply noticing beauty, but entertaining desire, feeding it in the mind, willfully imagining or pursuing it inwardly. “Already in his heart”: Jesus is not saying that the thought is identical to the physical act in consequence, but he is saying that the same sin begins in the heart. God judges the root, not just the fruit. The progression of sin matches James 1:14-15, where desire brings sin, and sin “bringeth forth death”. Adultery begins long before the actual act: in thought, in desire, in will. Jesus was correcting the Pharisaic mindset, which thought like: “I have not committed adultery, therefore I am righteous”. Yet Jesus says: “If thy heart is full of lust, thou art not clean.” God’s law is not merely about behavior, but about purity of heart.

“whosoever looketh on a woman(gynē) to lust after her…”: the Greek word used for woman is gynē, which can mean “woman” in general, or “wife” (depending on context). For example, in Jn 4:7 KJV: “There cometh a woman(gynē) of Samaria…” → clearly not “wife”, just a female person. But in Mt 1:20 KJV: “fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife(gynē)” → it is the same Greek word. So translators struggle to decide whether the woman to not lust after is a woman in general, or someone’s wife. Arguments for translating “woman”: (1) the text does not say: “his wife” or “another man’s wife”, just “woman”. (2) it is given in a universal statement paralleling “whosoever looketh..”, which suggest a general principle, not limited to married women; (3) Jesus is focusing on lust itself, addressing inner desire, not merely legal adultery categories; (4) the pattern in the context is to intensify the Law, where Jesus goes beyond physical adultery to heart-level purity, not narrowing, but expanding the command. The chapter finishes with “be perfect (v 48)”, therefore, Jesus could not have been endorsing lust towards non-married women. Arguments for translating “wife”: (1) the immediate context is adultery, which technically involves a wife; (2) the logical connection is defining “lust” as “intent toward adultery”, therefore the woman must be someone’s wife. Ultimately, most Bible translations choose “woman” because Jesus is demanding perfection in this chapter, so he could not be allowing lust towards non-married women in general as lust itself is listed as sinful elsewhere in Scripture. For example: “every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own LUST, and enticed. Then when LUST hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin…” (Jms 1:14-15 KJV), or “walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the LUST of the flesh. For the flesh LUSTETH against the Spirit…” (Gal 5:16-17 KJV), & “flee also youthful LUSTS…” (2 Tim 2:22 KJV), etc. Every lust is sinful because Scripture teaches that it begins inside (heart, mind, eyes), it leads to outward sin, it opposes the Spirit, it belongs to the fallen nature, and it must be fled and killed (Col 3:5). This sounds like an incredibly hard commandment, but so is perfection (v 48). Therefore: “with men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible” (Mt 19:26 KJV). Ultimately, the Christian goal is to not have “eyes of adultery” (2 Peter 2:14), which should be a reasonable ask for someone who claims to have been reborn in Christ. And we must never forget that: “not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us…” (Ti 3:5 KJV).

29-30.x: This portion is part of the same context of adultery and lusting (v 27-28), so they are part of the same warning about sin that begins in the heart. The phrase “offend thee” comes from the Greek “skandalizō,” which means “to cause to stumble”, or “to lead into sin”, or “to become a snare.” So Jesus is not speaking of mere annoyance, but of anything that may draw you into sin and endanger your soul. “Pluck it out… cut if off”: this is not literal, as sin comes from the heart (Mt 15:19), not merely from body parts. Removing an eye or cutting off a hand would not remove sinful desire. Hence, he is not commanding self-mutilation, but using hyperbole to emphasize how seriously sin must be dealt with. Sin is not a small matter, it leads to hell(from the Gk “gehenna”) if left unchecked. Better to lose something precious than to lose your soul. “If thy right eye.. If thy right hand..”: We must remove the source of temptation. The eye and the hand represent valuable, useful, beloved things. Yet if they lead us into sin, they must be cut off. Examples of this could be: bad habits, relationships, environments, and/or access to temptation like the internet & social media. Following Christ may require painful sacrifices like ending certain relationships, giving up pleasures of the flesh, changing one’s lifestyle, etc. But such loss is small compared to eternal ruin. This teaching is seen throughout Scripture: “Mortify therefore your members…” (Col 3:5 KJV); “Make no provision for the flesh…” (Rom 13:14 KJV); “Flee youthful lusts…” (2 Tim 2:22 KJV). So deal with sin decisively, immediately, and without mercy, even if it costs you something dear, for your soul is of far greater worth than anything you might lose.

Matthew 5:29-30 is one of those verses the institutionalized church used to justify the killing of “heretics,” where the “eye” or “hand” can mean a beloved brother, and the body the institutionalized church. Hence, in order to save the body from spreading, it was necessary to “cut off” (kill/burn) the “heretic.” Medieval canonists and inquisitorial rhetoric would use this imagery of removing corrupt members from the body to defend their actions, usually citing verses like: ““compel them to come in” (Lk 14:23 KJV); “A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Titus 3:10 KJV); & the laws in the book of Deuteronomy against false prophets: “And that prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, SHALL BE PUT TO DEATH; because he hath spoken to turn you away from the LORD your God…” (Deut 13:1-5 KJV) (other texts used were Deut 13:6-10, 12-15; 17:2-7; 18:20). In fact, one of the most popular and influential Catholic theologians, Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274AC), explicitly taught: “With regard to heretics … they deserve not only to be separated from the Church … but to be severed from the world BY DEATH. For it is a much graver matter to corrupt the faith … than to forge money … if … other evil-doers are condemned to death … much more reason is there for heretics, as soon as they are convicted of heresy, to be … put to death” (he also used forged Church Father quotations & Council Canons to argue for Papal Supremacy in his work Contra Errores Graecorum [Against the Errors of the Greeks]).

31-32.x: “It hath been said… But I say unto you:” Jesus continues to correct the wrong understanding of the Law. He is specifically addressing Deut 24:1 KJV: “When a man hath taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found some UNCLEANNESS(indecency) in her: then let him write her a bill of divorcement..” Many had interpreted this loosely, allowing divorce for almost any cause. So the focus shifted to: “as long as I give a document, it is lawful.” But Jesus brings the commandment back to its true intent: “whosoever shall put away his wife.. Causeth her to commit adultery.” The exception clause “saving for the cause of fornication.” The word “fornication” (Greek porneia, from where the word “porn” comes from), is an umbrella term for any number of illicit sexual activity, not just the one specific act of having sex outside of marriage. It also covers things like prostitution, adultery, incest, and other sexual acts that violate biblical-covenant boundaries. In some passages, porneia is used metaphorically to describe “spiritual adultery” or idolatry. For example, in Revelation, “Babylon’s fornication” symbolizes spiritual seduction and idolatrous alliance with worldly powers. In this context, Jesus is making divorce permissible only in the event of sexual sin from your partner (though not commanded). God himself forgives infidelity. In the book of Hosea, God commands the prophet Hosea to marry a woman who would be unfaithful to him (Hos 1:2), as a living illustration of God’s relationship with unfaithful Israel. Hosea married a woman named Gomer. She eventually left him and returned to a life of promiscuity, eventually ending up in slavery. After Gomer had abandoned Hosea and ruined her life, God commanded Hosea to go and buy her back from the slave market. This was to show that even though Israel (“the wife”) had “cheated” on God with idols, God still loved her and wanted her back (Hos 3:1). As Christians, our first instinct should never be divorce, but mercy, as taught by God.

33-37.x: “ye have heard.. But I say unto you”: Jesus gives the correct interpretation. In the culture of the time, people had developed a complex “legal loophole” system for lying. If they swore by God’s name, the oath was binding; but if they swore by “Heaven” or “Earth,” they felt they could break the promise without sinning. Jesus cuts right through it with a call for absolute, transparent honesty. “Shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths”: people thought that as long as you kept your vow to God, you were “legal”, disregarding any other promises. But Jesus shows the people that all those things that they swear by are still God’s territory, for example: (1) Heaven: don’t swear by it, for it is God’s throne; (2) Earth: don’t swear by it, for it is His footstool; (3) Jerusalem: Don’t swear by it, for it is the city of the Great King; (4) Your head: Don’t swear by your own life, because you don’t even have the power to change the color of your hair. The point is that everything in creation belongs to God, so you cannot invoke any part of the universe to back up your word because you don't own any of it, and breaking your promise would still count as taking God’s name in vain, as everything belongs to God. Your “Yes” should mean “Yes”, and your “No” should mean “No”. If you feel the need to say, “I swear on this or that”, it implies that your normal word isn’t trustworthy enough.

38-39.x: Jesus first quoted Exodus 21:24: “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth”. This was a legal principle for courts meant to limit retaliation, and it ensured the punishment was proportionate, not excessive. It was never meant for personal revenge, but had become treated that way. “Resist not evil.. Turn the other cheek”: this is not a command to allow all harm, but a correction of personal retaliation and pride. Jesus gives an example of being struck on the right cheek, being sued for a coat, and being compelled to go a mile. These are insults, minor offenses & social humiliation, not life-threatening violence. Jesus is teaching to not repay insult with insult, to not escalate conflict, and to be willing to endure wrong without revenge. He IS NOT commanding passive acceptance of murder or assault, nor the abolition of justice, nor the rejection of self-defense. Scripture elsewhere affirms the legitimacy of protecting life, such as: (1) defending one’s home (Ex 22:2); (2) preparation for danger (Lk 22:36), etc. The overall teaching is to not be ruled by vengeance, anger, or wounded pride. Instead, show restraint, mercy, absorb minor wrongs, and trust God for justice.

43-47.x: “Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy”: the first part is from Lev 19:18, but the “hate thine enemy” part was added as part of human tradition. The people had narrowed “neighbor” to mean only those like themselves & only those they favored. “Love your enemies.. Pray from them which despitefully use you..”: this is radical, it is not merely to avoid harming them, but to actively love them. “Love” in this context does not mean an emotion, but action and will: Bless them (speak good); Do good (act kindly); pray for them (seek their good before God). “That ye may be the children of your Father…”: this is a salvation issue, in order to become adopted by God, we must love our neighbor first: “for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” (1 Jn 4:20 KJV). It is much easier to claim to love an invisible, infinite God who never talks back or inconveniences you. If you cannot manage to love a physical human being standing right in front of you, your claim to love a spiritual Being is a lie. We must love our enemies because God Himself does: “He maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good..” (v 45). God shows common grace to all, therefore, his children must reflect His character. “If ye love them which love you, what reward have ye?”: Jesus points out that even tax collectors (despised sinners) do that, that even the world loves those who love them back - that requires no transformation. Kingdom righteousness must exceed ordinary human behavior. It is not enough to love friends or family members, true love actively tries to do good even to his enemies, and to those who are not able to reciprocate back. Love that only loves friends is ordinary, love that embraces enemies is divine.
